planting.note: Direct sow in fall into damp, saline-to-brackish, sandy or silty soil along marsh edges, ditches, and low coastal meadows, or set out spring divisions where a period of standing or seasonally wet soil can be provided.

directions: Direct sow in fall into damp, saline-to-brackish, sandy or silty soil along marsh edges, ditches, and low coastal meadows, or set out spring divisions where a period of standing or seasonally wet soil can be provided. This low, spreading aster tolerates salt spray and periodic tidal flooding that would kill most garden perennials, making it a workhorse for restoring pollinator habitat in Gulf Coast marsh fringes and brackish swales. Its late-season lavender ray flowers open from September into November, a critical nectar bridge for migrating monarchs and native bees just before frost. Cut back dead growth in late winter to encourage vigorous rebloom the following fall.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall so winter chilling breaks dormancy naturally, or set container transplants in fall or early spring into moist, acidic, sandy soil typical of longleaf pine flatwoods and savanna edges.

directions: Sow seed in fall so winter chilling breaks dormancy naturally, or set container transplants in fall or early spring into moist, acidic, sandy soil typical of longleaf pine flatwoods and savanna edges. This clump-forming aster stays low and grass-like most of the year, then sends up wide lavender-blue daisy flowers in late summer and fall that draw abundant native bees, skippers, and late-season butterflies. It performs best where competing vegetation is periodically cut back or burned, mimicking the fire regime of its native pine savanna habitat. Avoid rich, heavily amended soil, which encourages floppy growth and rot.

planting.note: Surface-sow in fall onto dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soil in full sun, pressing seed in but leaving it exposed to light since it is a light-dependent germinator that should not be buried deeply.

directions: Surface-sow in fall onto dry, sandy, nutrient-poor soil in full sun, pressing seed in but leaving it exposed to light since it needs light to germinate; established plants spread gently by rhizome to form loose colonies. Despite the common name it is not a true Solidago but a close goldenrod relative with narrow, resinous, aromatic leaves and flat-topped clusters of small gold flowers from late summer into fall. It is an exceptional late-season nectar source for migrating monarchs, native bees, and beneficial wasps, and thrives on the dry sandy ridges and pine barrens of the coastal plain where richer-soil goldenrods struggle. Deadhead spent flower heads if self-seeding is not wanted, as it can colonize open sandy sites readily.
sources: Alabama Plant Atlas (University of West Alabama)

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed in spring into deep, dry, infertile sand; this coastal-plain wildflower is built for droughty, excessively drained dunes and scrub and will rot in average garden soil.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed in spring into deep, dry, infertile sand — this coastal-plain wildflower is built for droughty, excessively drained dunes and scrub and will rot in average garden soil. Its wiry stems carry bright yellow, ball-like flower heads made of distinctive papery, honeycomb-textured bracts from summer through fall, attracting a steady stream of small native bees, skippers, and beneficial wasps. It reseeds readily on bare sandy ground and is a favorite of coastal restoration plantings in Florida and along the Gulf shore. Give it full, unobstructed sun and avoid mulch or irrigation once established, since both encourage fungal problems.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring, or set out divisions, into consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy soil such as roadside ditches, wet pine savannas, and pond margins.

directions: Direct sow in early spring, or set out divisions, into consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy soil such as roadside ditches, wet pine savannas, and pond margins. This low rosette-forming fleabane sends up airy stems topped with abundant small white-rayed, yellow-centered flowers in spring and early summer, providing an early nectar source for small native bees and syrphid flies before many summer wildflowers begin blooming. It spreads modestly by short rhizomes and self-seeding to form loose drifts in wet meadow plantings. Keep soil damp through establishment; it does not tolerate prolonged drought once mature growth has begun.
